content: 1. A study conducted in Russia compared baby-led breastfeeding with scheduled or mixed breastfeeding to evaluate its impact on breastfeeding success in healthy newborns. This trial involved 176 women but did not meet the inclusion criteria for further analysis. 2. A review by Watson and McGuire (2016) assessed the effects of responsive feeding versus scheduled feeding in preterm infants. Nine randomized controlled trials involving 593 infants were included, but none reported critical outcomes such as growth rates, parental satisfaction, or time to hospital discharge. The studies originated from Canada and the United States. 3. Smith and Becker (2016) reviewed the benefits and risks of introducing additional foods or fluids to healthy, full-term, breastfed infants under six months of age. Eleven trials with 2,542 mother-infant pairs from the Czech Republic, Sweden, and the United States were analyzed. 4. Jaafar et al. (2016) examined the impact of restricted versus unrestricted pacifier use on breastfeeding duration and outcomes in healthy, full-term newborns. Three trials involving 1,915 babies from Argentina, Canada, and Switzerland were included. 5. Foster et al. (2016) evaluated the effects of non-nutritive sucking on physiological stability and nutrition in preterm infants. Twelve trials with 746 preterm infants from Australia, Brazil, China, the United Kingdom, and the United States were reviewed. 6. Greene et al. (2016) investigated the effectiveness of oral stimulation interventions in promoting oral feeding in preterm infants born before 37 weeks of gestation. Nineteen trials with 823 participants from Brazil, China, France, India, Iran, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. 7. Flint et al. (2016) compared cup feeding with other forms of enteral feeding for term and preterm infants unable to fully breastfeed. Five trials with 971 participants from Australia, Brazil, Turkey, and the United Kingdom were analyzed. 8. Collins et al. (2016) reviewed the avoidance of bottle feeding during the establishment of breastfeeding in preterm infants. Seven trials with 1,152 participants from Australia, Brazil, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. 9. Abe et al. (2016) assessed whether hospitals with written breastfeeding policies were more likely to implement the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding and improve breastfeeding rates and duration. One study involving 916 infants from Brazil was included. 10. Gavine et al. (2017) evaluated the impact of education and training programs for healthcare staff on their knowledge, attitudes, and skills in supporting breastfeeding women. Three trials with 250 participants from Brazil, Denmark, and Sweden were analyzed. 11. Balogun et al. (2017) reviewed the effects of training facility-based health workers on breastfeeding outcomes. Six studies with 390 health workers from Australia, Brazil, Canada, Sweden, and the United States were included. 12. Lumbiganon et al. (2016) examined the effectiveness of antenatal breastfeeding education in increasing breastfeeding initiation and duration. Twenty-four trials with 10,056 women from Australia, Canada, China, Denmark, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and the United States were analyzed. 13. Balogun et al. (2016) evaluated the effectiveness of various breastfeeding promotion interventions in increasing breastfeeding initiation rates. Twenty-eight trials with 107,362 women from Ghana, Malawi, Nicaragua, Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. 14. Da Silva Lopez et al. (2016) reviewed the importance of providing linkage to breastfeeding support groups after hospital discharge to improve breastfeeding outcomes. Two cluster-randomized controlled trials with 5,590 mother-infant pairs from Australia and the Democratic Republic of Congo were analyzed. 15. The use of formalized instruments to assess preterm infants' readiness to feed by breast or bottle was explored. Instruments such as the Dynamic-Early Feeding Scale (D-EFS), Early Feeding Skills (EFS), and Neonatal Oral Motor Assessment Scale (NOMAS) were identified, but none were tested in experimental studies. 16. Several studies reported on the volume of milk expressed during different sessions over three days. The findings indicated slight increases in milk volume, but the evidence quality was low due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. 17. The GRADE system was used to evaluate the quality of evidence across studies. Evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low quality based on factors such as risk of bias, heterogeneity, and imprecision. This summary highlights the scope, methodologies, and findings of various studies and reviews related to breastfeeding practices, interventions, and outcomes.
